chapters.title: Other people’s perspectives and our own afflictions

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I’ll clarify a point, and then you guys think of your hard questions. We talked earlier about not rejecting other worldviews. What’s the difference between accepting and rejecting?

I said that to not block yourself from omniscience, you have to entertain that other people see things differently than you. There are sixty-three people on this Zoom call, so there are sixty-three realities happening right now. But there are actually more realities than that, because there’s Tim’s reality and Tim’s interpretation of the other sixty-two people’s realities. Then there’s Roxanna and Roxanna’s interpretation of the other sixty-two people.
There aren’t sixty-three perspectives on this call. There are way more potential realities. The point is to understand where things are coming from.

Right now I’m looking at Isabel. Isabel looks like an outside person. She’s doing her own thing, living her own life. She has her own set of experiences. I don’t know anything about Isabel’s childhood. I met her maybe six years ago. I know she’s a translator. I know some things about her life. We’ve shared programs together.

She’s a bunch of seeds. She’s a bunch of experience that’s gone from beginning to now. I don’t know when the beginning was. She’s an outside person, and she’s coming from me. She has a full life. It’s not like Isabel goes away and disappears from my life and her life isn’t happening.

This is where it gets confusing. People say, “If I’m not perceiving it, it didn’t happen. If I’m not there to perceive the tree falling in the forest, did it make a sound?” The answer is yes, because somebody can perceive it.

There are certain kinds of seeds that don’t really ripen in my day-to-day life anymore, or very infrequently. But I see them in other people. My main affliction isn’t really anger. I do get little bumps of anger during the day, but it’s not the thing that really hurts me as much as other afflictions.

When I see certain things in other people that are their worst affliction, it’s wrong worldview for me to think, “I don’t have that. That’s not me. I’m better than that anger. I don’t get angry like that.”
Wrong. No. It means it’s still there. If you’re capable of perceiving it in your world, it means it’s coming from you.

Do I accept if somebody is angry? Do I reject their anger? If I see someone treating someone poorly because they get angry at them all the time, or they’re constantly looking for a reason to be angry, do I accept their anger? Do I reject their anger?

First of all, it’s coming from me. “All right, dude”—I’m talking to myself—“this is coming from me. In subtle ways, I have done this or I still do this. Let’s work on changing that behavior. Stop it. Just stop, Tim. Thank you, person X, for showing me that I still have those seeds.”

Does that mean I let that person stay angry and continue to hurt people? No. I try to calm them down. I give them cookies, love, respect. If that doesn’t work, I ignore them. If that doesn’t work, I create boundaries and say, “Look, you can’t do this anymore. You can’t participate in my world anymore. That’s not kind. I will not let you be mean to other people.”
That’s a hard thing about being a director of organizations. You have to create policies. Sometimes you have to say no to people. You can still love them.
That’s the same answer to whether I accept or reject someone who believes in Zeus. Wrong question. How do you treat them?

If someone thinks there’s a god on a mountain controlling tornadoes, does it help them? Does it hurt them? Does it hurt others? Does it help others? You have to live in the world. You can’t just ignore the world.

It becomes really hard when you see things in your world and it’s a broken realm. If you think things are self-existent, if you think they’re coming from their own side, it’s going to be broken and continue to be broken.

It can be uncomfortable to navigate, because if I really lived up to my ethical standards, I wouldn’t ever get in a car. I’m stealing oil from the earth. I’m hitting bugs the whole way. If I did that, I wouldn’t be able to live.
So accepting and rejecting is not the most helpful frame. How do you help that person? They’re outside of you, yes. Stop being angry yourself. But if you’re angry, how do you want to be treated?

Most times people who are angry are not angry at the thing they look angry at. They need something else. They need support. Maybe they were abused when they were younger. Maybe they weren’t taken care of. Maybe they didn’t get the love they needed or wanted.

For me, a lot of my reactions are because of certain things that happened to me. They have nothing to do with the person in front of me. Karmically speaking, they have nothing to do with it anyway. But we have patterns and habits in our lives.
How can we soften our minds and hearts to other people’s perspectives, even if we think they’re wrong? Then you have to evaluate: why do I think it’s wrong?
If this person is upset and angry at everything, maybe they want community. Maybe they want to be included. The anger is annoying. But how can you help them?
That’s where the *bodhichitta* comes in. How do you soften to everyone? How do you soften in the face of everyone else’s stuff? Because it’s yours. It’s yours anyway.

If you truly understood that everything is coming from you, how would you treat your mental afflictions? If someone is doing something outside of you that hurts other people, and you truly understood that’s your affliction, how would you treat that?
We give ourselves so many passes. “It’s okay, Tim. You can lie today. It’s okay. You can be difficult today. You didn’t sleep well. You didn’t eat well. You’re overworked and underpaid.”
But when somebody else is overworked, underpaid, tired, and hungry, we don’t put up with their behavior. We judge them.
If you truly understood where things come from, how would you treat your projections? How would you treat that movie in your holodeck?

It’s helpful if you understand it’s all in your *kunshi* [`KUN GZHI`] and that’s all you’re seeing. That brings about a tremendous amount of personal responsibility. The Mind Only School creates an incredible sense of personal responsibility. Then take that into the Upper Middle Way. Take that personal responsibility out of that mind with you from the Mind Only School into the Upper Middle Way.

chapters.title: Study, family, and the path back to others

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Ella asks: “I have this deep passion for studying and learning all this stuff about seeds and emptiness”—she called it Diamond Wisdom—“but it kind of takes away from my passion to serve my family, the people closest to me.”

I wouldn’t judge yourself. I think it’s a normal part of the path. If you become very passionate about one thing, sometimes you lose passion for others. But don’t forget that the path will lead you back to other people eventually anyway.

Sometimes we have to take care of ourselves. Sometimes we have to go into deep retreat. Make sure you’re not hurting people. You’ve already made a commitment to your family. Don’t break that commitment. But maybe you can plant seeds that give you the time to study more.

If anyone wants to do a seed-planting project on how to keep getting new projects and do all of them, and study and do retreat, reach out to me. I have a problem. I don’t know how I’m going to be a Mixed Nut now. I have no idea how I’m going to do this. So let’s plant some seeds for time.
The answer is that the path always leads back to other people. Sometimes we have to take a break, but it always goes back to other people.
